text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Four niche banks have reported their larger competitors to the Swedish competition authorities for allegedly charging too much for access to the country's nationwide network of automatic cash dispensers.
- One woman died and two more were seriously ill after being infected by a virulent bacteria in a maternity ward at a Stockholm hospital.
- Now is the time to fix mortgage interest rates. All indicators suggest that the prolonged fall in interest rates over the spring and summer has bottomed out.

- Almost a thousand employees of bearing manufacturer SKF have bought IBM personal computers at knock-down rates through a deal organised by the engineering union. SKF is subsidising IT training for all of the employees involved.
- Parts of Stockholm's national city park, the first of its kind in the world, have been sold to an individual accused of building illegally in the protected green area around the Swedish capital.
- Swedish bond yields have not followed those in Italy and Spain lower as closely as in the past because of nerves over Swedish membership in the European Union's monetary union.
- Swedish banks continue to post higher profits, but the pace of the improvement is slowing.

- Telecoms group Ericsson temporarily edged past drug company Astra to become the largest firm by market value listed on the Stockholm bourse at 185 billion crowns. The share price fell, however, by session-end on Wednesday.
- Sweden is the world's second most advanced country after the United States in terms of information technology, a report shows.
- Salus, an insurance and finance company owned by an association of Swedish doctors, plans to apply for a listing on the Stockholm share market next year.
